newsitem.title: INDIA: India says no change in Suzuki car venture stake.
newsitem.headline: India says no change in Suzuki car venture stake.

text.p: The Indian government said on Friday that it had decided not to allow a change in the equity structure of carmaker Maruti Udyog Ltd in which the Indian government and Japan's Suzuki Motor Company hold 50 pct each.
"The present position will continue," Industry Minister Murasoli Maran said in reply to a question at a news conference. "There won't be any change in the equity level."
Analysts say Suzuki wants to increase its stake.

Automobile experts said India's stance may raise costs for Suzuki, which has been keen to consolidate the 70 percent market share of the Indian car market it grabbed with a headstart in the early 1980s when India still followed socialist policies.
Suzuki says it is keen to increase its hold on Maruti to compete with several global giants which have entered India under an economic reform programme launched in 1991.
At stake is a 15 billion rupee ($418 million) expansion plan by Maruti to increase production capacity to 450,000 units a year from the current 350,000.
"Demand is growing. Unless and until they produce, somebody else will take the market," said a Bombay-based automobile industry analyst, who asked not to be named.
Another analyst said if Suzuki was not allowed to increase its share in the joint venture, the government would have to contribute to an increase in overall equity.
If Suzuki cannot raise its stake, it might be forced to borrow or raise funds through securities not listed in India, said K.N. Sreenivasan of fund manager Jardine Fleming.
"Taking on a debt like that is a big burden. When the competitive heat increases, the profit margins suffer."
Maran spoke as a delegation of the powerful Japan Federation of Economic Organisations (Keidanren) started a week-long visit to New Delhi in an effort to consolidate Japanese investments.
South Korea's Daewoo Motor Co, Ford Motor Corp and General Motors Co of the United States, France's Peugeot and Japan's Honda and Toyota are among firms that have entered India since 1991.
Indian newspapers have said that the government wants to replace Maruti Udyog's current managing director, R.C. Bhargava, who is favoured by Suzuki.
Maran said the question of choosing a new managing director for Maruti would not be taken up until August.
Suzuki, without confirming it was seeking a higher stake, said last month that it was in talks with the Indian government on who should take the lead in running Maruti.

"We need quick decision-making in the Indian automobile market to improve competitiveness, as other foreign carmakers are going to enter the Indian market," company president Osamu Suzuki said in Tokyo.
Suzuki said in a full-page advertisement in the Economic Times, India's leading business daily, on Friday that it wanted to strengthen Maruti.

"To prevail in the severe business climate, Suzuki, a holder of 50 percent of Maruti stock, believes that Maruti will be further strengthened by adding to the professional and business expertise in the management," it said.

Maruti Udyog has set a production target of 320,000 vehicles and exports of 30,000 in the 1996/97 financial year ending on March 31. It reported net profit of 4.09 billion rupees ($114.2 million) for 1995/96, up from 2.48 billion in the previous year.
($1=35.8 rupees)
